newsitem.title: MEXICO: Telmex's Q2 results -- glass half-empty or full?
newsitem.headline: Telmex's Q2 results -- glass half-empty or full?

text.p: Mexican telephone giant Telefonos de Mexico turned in mixed second quarter results that raised more questions than they answered about the company's ability to fend off its new rivals.
While the company's quarterly earnings fell short of expectations, its operating results as a whole were slightly better than forecast, analysts said.
"I would still be neutral on Telmex. There were some reasons to be encouraged ... but also some things to worry about," Robert Hulme, analyst at Interacciones in New York, told Reuters.
Telmex reported earnings per share of about 77.5 cents per ADR -- below 80 cents per ADR, the average predicted by four analysts interviewed by Reuters last week.
As expected, revenues fell slightly compared to the same quarter of last year as new competitors in long-distance services lowered prices in a bid to win customers.
Quarterly revenues were 13.626 billion pesos versus 13.72 billion during the year-ago quarter.

But with the exception of weaker margins, analysts said revenues and operating profits held up better than expected. Higher rates boosted local service sales and lower long-distance tariffs raised volumes over a year ago, when Telmex still had a monopoly.
"I think (Wall Street) can be pleased with how they performed operationally during the quarter," Luis Carvalho at Morgan Stanley told Reuters.
Carvalho said he thought a weak bottom line was due mostly to higher tax payments during the quarter.
"During the first two quarters, tax payments have averaged 40 percent. For the year, I expect them to average 37.5 percent," he said.

Other analysts said weak margins were due to a 3.1 percent jump in operating costs -- due to a combination of stepped-up advertising, a roughly 20 percent wage rise in April, and the costs of connecting new competitors to its local network.
"Revenues and operating profits were as expected, but we miscalculated operating expenses," a Mexico City analyst who declined to be named said.
Telmex faced its first serious competition during the quarter as most of the country opened its doors to the former monopoly's new rivals.

The competitors include Alestra, a joint venture between AT&T. Mexican industrial conglomerate Alfa and holding group VISA-Bancomer. Another rival is Avantel, a joint venture between MCI Communications and Mexico's financial group Banamex-Accival.

Long-distance prices may have fallen faster than expected, some analysts said. International long-distance revenues per minute -- a rough estimate of price -- were about 2.85 pesos versus 3.36 pesos in the first quarter.
The Mexico City analyst was disappointed that Telmex's international long-distance volumes fell about one percent during the second quarter versus the first, despite lower prices.
Others like Hulme said Telmex held up well considering it had lost about 25 percent of the long-distance market.
"These results reflect the advent of competition in the second quarter. And I see a downward trend in terms of minutes volume and average prices," said Hulme.
"However, the long-distance market in general will probably show some strength due to the economy and lower prices will spur volume," he added.
Carvalho said he did not think long-distance prices had much more room to fall, and saw more upside for local tariffs to take up the slack on revenues.
